steps.message: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: Our test suite grew big and we haven't noticed how the total RSpec run time outgrew 10 minutes (no parallelization) on CI.

We need to profile the test suite and identify the common problems (shared by many specs) and fix them once and for all. Keep refactoring of individual examples minimal: prefer configuration- and setup-level changes — adding tags, restructuring shared setup, wrapping execution. What the examples assert must stay the same. No app code changes affecting runtime behavior.

NOTE: Running the whole test suite is very time-consuming. Don't try to run the whole test suite (it would fail with timeout due to the Bash tool limitations) or even multiple directories. Only `rspec spec/<some-folder>`. Completely ignore system specs and streaming related specs (we do not run them by default anyway).

We will work on specific spec types at each optimization phase: `spec/models` and `spec/requests`. In the end, we want these two groups together to run at least twice as fast as they do today. Store any insights/comments/plans (such as baseline metrics) that could be useful for the future runs in the docs/ folder (so you can use that knowledge during future optimization runs).

We've already made the first run of optimizations affecting only `spec/models` tests. Let's now profile and optimize the second group—`spec/requests`. Do not touch factories yet — we will work on them later.

We anticipate a similar speed-up of >30% compared to the baseline (captured at the previous step, before any optimization work). Note that optimizations made for models could have already improved requests specs enough. If that's the case, look for request-specific bottlenecks to get the rest of the way there.

{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output_head": "# RSpec performance notes

Living document for the effort to bring the RSpec run time down (it had grown past
10 minutes on CI without parallelization). Keep it up to date when you run another
optimization phase: add measurements to the "Results log" and new findings to
"Findings", so the next run does not have to rediscover them.

## Scope and status

| Phase | Scope | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `spec/models` (target: >= 30-35% faster) | Done: about 62-66% faster (2.6-3x), see "Results log" |
| 2 | `spec/requests` (target: `spec/models` + `spec/requests` together >= 2x faster than the original baseline) | Not started |
| 3 | Factories (`spec/fabricators`; "do not touch" until this phase) | Not started |

Ignored everywhere: `spec/system` and streaming-related specs.

Rules followed in phase 1:
- No app code changes. Only spec configuration, spec support and one stray spec line.
- No changes to what examples assert. Examples were not refactored.
- Factories untouched.
- Other spec types (`spec/requests`, etc.) were not optimized, but note that some
  changes are process-wide (see "Process-wide changes").

## How to measure

- Run one folder at a time: `bundle exec rspec spec/models`. Never run the whole
  suite in this environment (it times out).
- Never run two spec processes at the same time. They share the `mastodon_test`
  database and the local Redis, so results are wrong and noisy.
- Use a fixed seed so runs are comparable, and compare at least two seeds. Run
  order is random by default. The `.rspec`/config do not fix the seed.
- Record the example time from RSpec's summary ("Finished in ...") and the wall
  time (`time`). Expect about 2 s of boot on top of the example time.
- Single-run noise is roughly +/-5%. Use two or more seeds before concluding.
- JSON output for per-example analysis:
  `bundle exec rspec spec/models --seed 4242 --format progress --format json --out /tmp/models.json`
  - `summary.duration` is the example time.
  - `examples[].run_time` and `examples[].file_path` give the per-file breakdown.
- Profiling with StackProf, without touching the repo. Put this in a file outside the
  repo and load it with `-r` (`stackprof` is in the bundle):

  ```ruby
  # /tmp/stackprof_hook.rb
  require 'stackprof'
  StackProf.start(mode: :cpu, interval: 500, raw: true)
  at_exit { StackProf.stop; StackProf.results(ENV.fetch('STACKPROF_OUT', '/tmp/models.dump')) }
  ```

  ```sh
  STACKPROF_OUT=/tmp/models_cpu.dump bundle exec rspec spec/models -r /tmp/stackprof_hook.rb --seed 4242
  bundle exec stackprof /tmp/models_cpu.dump --text --limit 40        # self time
  bundle exec stackprof /tmp/models_cpu.dump --method 'Some#method'   # callers/callees
  ```

  Profiling adds roughly 3-5% overhead, so do not use profiled runs for the numbers.
  Inclusive % (frames that appear anywhere on the stack) was the most useful view:
  parse the raw dump with `Marshal.load` and count each frame once per sample.

## Environment (baseline and phase 1)

- aarch64 Linux container, Ruby 4.0.6 (YJIT compiled in, disabled by default),
  Rails 8.1.3.1, RSpec 3.13 / rspec-rails 8.0.4, Sidekiq 8.1.6 (`Sidekiq::Testing`
  inline mode in specs), Devise 5.0.4, Fabrication 3.0.0, WebMock 3.26.
- PostgreSQL and Redis on localhost. The DB is `mastodon_test`.
- CPU-bound: `user` time is about equal to wall time, so DB/Redis round trips are
  not the bottleneck. CPU in Ruby is.

## Baseline (original code)

`spec/models`: 152 files, 1795 examples, 0 failures.

| Seed | Example time | Wall time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4242 | 123.85 s | 2m05.8s |
| 1234 | 124.96 s | - |
| 98765 | 133.25 s | - |

Per-example run time (seed 4242): median 26 ms, p90 174 ms, p99 718 ms, max 3.0 s,
min 1.2 ms. Hook overhead for a trivial example is about 0.7 ms (measured with 500
empty examples), so per-example hooks are not a problem by themselves.

Slowest files at baseline (total example time):

| File | Time | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `account_statuses_cleanup_policy_spec.rb` | 11.9 s | 36 |
| `trends/statuses_spec.rb` | 10.8 s | 12 |
| `tag_feed_spec.rb` | 9.9 s | 33 |
| `status_spec.rb` | 9.1 s | 62 |
| `public_feed_spec.rb` | 6.3 s | 43 |
| `notification_spec.rb` | 5.8 s | 25 |
| `media_attachment_spec.rb` | 5.6 s | 27 |
| `concerns/status/threading_concern_spec.rb` | 5.2 s | 16 |

Slowest single example: `MediaAttachment mp3 with large cover art` (2.7 s, real
7.8 MB fixture, asserts real metadata extraction, so it is kept as-is).

## Findings

Ordered by share of CPU in the baseline profile. Shares are of total samples,
inclusive unless noted.

1. **Verbose query logs were on for the whole process (about 35% of CPU).**
   `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb` ran
   `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` at describe level. That line runs at
   file load, so it applies to the whole run, and nothing turned it back off. With
   the flag on, every SQL statement captures a caller backtrace and cleans it with
   ",
  "output_tail": "out 2% Premailer).*
     Devise notifications render HTML and inline CSS. Changing that would change what
     specs see in mail bodies.
   - *Media/image processing (Paperclip, Vips, ffmpeg, about 3%).* Specs assert on
     real thumbnails and metadata. Keep.
   - *App validators that query the DB for each user (`UsernameBlock`,
     `EmailDomainBlock`, `UnreservedUsernameValidator`, `UniqueUsernameValidator`,
     about 9% combined, inclusive, overlapping parts not summed).* App code, so not touched.
   - *`Setting` reads (about 2-4%).* `config.after` clears `Rails.cache` after every
     example. Keeping the cache across examples would return rolled-back settings, so
     this stays.
   - *Fabricators (out of scope until phase 3).* `account` fabricator builds a `user`
     for every local account. `status` fabricator builds an account when none is given
     and creates a bookmark in `after_create`. Inclusive cost in the phase-1 profile:
     the `status` fabricator's `after_create` bookmark block about 18%, the `account`
     fabricator's `user` build about 9%.
     The `account` fabricator attaches a precomputed keypair, so RSA key generation
     (`Account#generate_keys`, about 19 ms per key) is avoided. Keep it that way.
   - *Redis (about 5% of CPU).* Mostly the inline Sidekiq jobs and counters. Not
     pursued.

## Changes made in phase 1

- `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb`: removed the load-time
  `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` line (finding 1).
- `spec/support/test_performance.rb` (new): per-example verbose-log guard (finding 1),
  webhook job skip for model specs (finding 2), memoized Devise digests for model
  specs (finding 3).
- `spec/spec_helper.rb`: YJIT enabled when available (finding 4).

### Process-wide changes

The YJIT enable in `spec/spec_helper.rb` is process-wide, so `spec/requests` gets faster
now too. The verbose-log guard does nothing unless something sets the flag. The webhook
skip and the digest memo are scoped to `type: :model`, so they do not change other spec
types yet. When
phase 2 starts, measure the `spec/requests` baseline from the original commit (stash
the phase-1 changes) or the phase-2 gains will be misattributed.

## Results log

Example time from RSpec's "Finished in" line for `spec/models`. All runs: 1795
examples, 0 failures, same seed where listed.

| Change set | Seed 4242 | Seed 1234 | Seed 98765 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Original code | 123.85 s | 124.96 s | 133.25 s |
| + verbose logs off (finding 1) | 74.93 s | - | - |
| + webhook skip (finding 2) | 54.15 s | - | - |
| + YJIT (finding 4) | 48.08 s | - | - |
| + Devise digest memo (finding 3), final | 47.33 s | 46.01 s | 44.95 s |
| Final code, re-run | 45.23 s (wall 47.8 s) | - | - |

Final: about 62-66% less example time (2.6-3x faster). Target for phase 1 was 30-35%.

Per-file example time after the change (seed 4242): `media_attachment_spec.rb`
5.3 s, `account_statuses_cleanup_policy_spec.rb` 3.4 s, `trends/statuses_spec.rb` 2.7 s,
`status_spec.rb` 2.6 s, `tag_feed_spec.rb` 2.4 s, `public_feed_spec.rb` 2.1 s.

## Plan for next phases

- **Phase 2 (`spec/requests`).** Measure the `spec/requests` baseline on the original
  commit first. The request specs create many users, statuses and accounts, so the
  webhook skip and the digest memo could help a lot. Consider widening them from
  `type: :model` to all types, after checking each spec type's assertions (webhook
  delivery assertions, query counts). Check `spec/requests` for request-level
  webhook expectations before widening.
- **Phase 3 (factories).** The biggest remaining costs are in fabricators:
  `account` builds a `user` for each local account, `status` builds an account and
  adds a bookmark in `after_create`. Lazy or shared defaults could avoid unneeded
  rows, but they change what gets created, so review per fabricator.
- **Optional, cheap, not done:** detach AR SQL logging in test (about 7%), tune GC via
  environment in CI (not measured), and `WebhookService#call` early return (app code,
  needs approval).
- **Parallelization** is out of scope here (`bin/flatware rspec` exists in CI).

## Gotchas

- Don't run spec processes in parallel: they share `mastodon_test` and Redis.
- `log/test.log` grows by tens of MB per `spec/models` run because SQL is logged, and
  it is never truncated between runs. It is git-ignored. Clear it if disk I/O matters
  for an experiment.
- The webhook skip changes SQL query counts inside blocks that create users or
  statuses, because the webhook job's queries are no longer executed. No spec in
  `spec/models` counts queries across such a block today. Re-check when widening it.
- `execute_queries` matchers (`spec/support/matchers/sql_queries.rb`) count all SQL
  in a block, so they also see those queries.
- To compare with the original code, stash only the phase-1 files
  (`git stash push --include-untracked`). Ignored artifacts like `tmp/` and
  `log/` do not need to move.

# Configuration-level guards that keep the test suite fast.
# Background, baseline metrics and the optimization plan live in docs/rspec-performance.md.

RSpec.configure do |config|
  # Verbose query logs make ActiveRecord capture and clean a backtrace for every
  # SQL statement the suite runs (~35% of spec/models CPU time). The Rails default
  # is `false`; nothing in the suite asserts on log output, so keep it off per
  # example, even if a spec file flips the global at load time.
  config.before do
    ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = false
  end

  # Creating a local User or Status enqueues TriggerWebhookWorker, which Sidekiq
  # runs inline in specs. WebhookService serializes the event *before* looking up
  # enabled webhooks, so in most specs (no enabled webhook) ~25% of spec/models CPU
  # went into building a payload that is never delivered. When no webhook is
  # enabled the job has no observable effect, so skip it. Specs that create an
  # enabled webhook still run the real pipeline. Specs that stub perform_async
  # themselves are unaffected, since their stubs are defined after this one.
  config.before(:each, type: :model) do
    allow(TriggerWebhookWorker).to receive(:perform_async).and_wrap_original do |original, *args|
      original.call(*args) if Webhook.enabled.exists?
    end
  end

  # Devise bcrypt-hashes the password of every user built by a fabricator (~1.2ms
  # each, even at bcrypt's minimum cost of 4), and local accounts build a user too,
  # so a spec/models run hashed ~3000 times. Specs only use a few passwords, and
  # `valid_password?` still verifies a memoized digest, so reuse one digest per
  # (model, pepper, stretches, password). Only the random salt is shared.
  password_digests = {}
  config.before(:each, type: :model) do
    allow(Devise::Encryptor).to receive(:digest).and_wrap_original do |original, klass, password|
      password_digests[[klass, klass.pepper, klass.stretches, password]] ||= original.call(klass, password)
    end
  end
end

{
  "returncode": 0,
  "output": "- Profiling with StackProf, without touching the repo. Put this in a file outside the
  repo and load it with `-r` (`stackprof` is in the bundle):

  ```ruby
  # /tmp/stackprof_hook.rb
  require 'stackprof'
  StackProf.start(mode: :cpu, interval: 500, raw: true)
  at_exit { StackProf.stop; StackProf.results(ENV.fetch('STACKPROF_OUT', '/tmp/models.dump')) }
  ```

  ```sh
  STACKPROF_OUT=/tmp/models_cpu.dump bundle exec rspec spec/models -r /tmp/stackprof_hook.rb --seed 4242
  bundle exec stackprof /tmp/models_cpu.dump --text --limit 40        # self time
  bundle exec stackprof /tmp/models_cpu.dump --method 'Some#method'   # callers/callees
  ```

  Profiling adds roughly 3-5% overhead, so do not use profiled runs for the numbers.
  Inclusive % (frames that appear anywhere on the stack) was the most useful view:
  parse the raw dump with `Marshal.load` and count each frame once per sample.

## Environment (baseline and phase 1)

- aarch64 Linux container, Ruby 4.0.6 (YJIT compiled in, disabled by default),
  Rails 8.1.3.1, RSpec 3.13 / rspec-rails 8.0.4, Sidekiq 8.1.6 (`Sidekiq::Testing`
  inline mode in specs), Devise 5.0.4, Fabrication 3.0.0, WebMock 3.26.
- PostgreSQL and Redis on localhost. The DB is `mastodon_test`.
- CPU-bound: `user` time is about equal to wall time, so DB/Redis round trips are
  not the bottleneck. CPU in Ruby is.

## Baseline (original code)

`spec/models`: 152 files, 1795 examples, 0 failures.

| Seed | Example time | Wall time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4242 | 123.85 s | 2m05.8s |
| 1234 | 124.96 s | - |
| 98765 | 133.25 s | - |

Per-example run time (seed 4242): median 26 ms, p90 174 ms, p99 718 ms, max 3.0 s,
min 1.2 ms. Hook overhead for a trivial example is about 0.7 ms (measured with 500
empty examples), so per-example hooks are not a problem by themselves.

Slowest files at baseline (total example time):

| File | Time | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `account_statuses_cleanup_policy_spec.rb` | 11.9 s | 36 |
| `trends/statuses_spec.rb` | 10.8 s | 12 |
| `tag_feed_spec.rb` | 9.9 s | 33 |
| `status_spec.rb` | 9.1 s | 62 |
| `public_feed_spec.rb` | 6.3 s | 43 |
| `notification_spec.rb` | 5.8 s | 25 |
| `media_attachment_spec.rb` | 5.6 s | 27 |
| `concerns/status/threading_concern_spec.rb` | 5.2 s | 16 |

Slowest single example: `MediaAttachment mp3 with large cover art` (2.7 s, real
7.8 MB fixture, asserts real metadata extraction, so it is kept as-is).

## Findings

Ordered by share of CPU in the baseline profile. Shares are of total samples,
inclusive unless noted.

1. **Verbose query logs were on for the whole process (about 35% of CPU).**
   `spec/models/concerns/status/fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb` ran
   `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = true` at describe level. That line runs at
   file load, so it applies to the whole run, and nothing turned it back off. With
   the flag on, every SQL statement captures a caller backtrace and cleans it with
   `ActiveSupport::BacktraceCleaner` (`Thread.each_caller_location`, `String#sub`).
   The Rails default is `false`.
   *Fix:* the stray line was removed (the examples never asserted on logs), and
   `spec/support/test_performance.rb` resets the flag before each example, so a
   future load-time assignment cannot leak into other examples.

2. **Webhook jobs run inline for every local User and Status (about 25% of CPU).**
   `User` (`after_create_commit`) and `Status` (`after_create_commit`/`after_update_commit`)
   enqueue `TriggerWebhookWorker`. Sidekiq inline mode runs it immediately.
   `WebhookService#call` serializes the whole event (REST admin serializer, account
   counters, roles, and so on) *before* it asks which webhooks are enabled. In a
   normal spec, no webhook is enabled, so that payload is built and dropped.
   *Fix (spec-only):* `spec/support/test_performance.rb` wraps
   `TriggerWebhookWorker.perform_async` for `type: :model` and calls it only if
   `Webhook.enabled.exists?`. Specs that stub `perform_async` themselves
   (`user_spec.rb`, `user/confirmation_spec.rb`) are unaffected, because their stubs
   are defined later. Specs that enable a webhook still run the real pipeline.
   *Candidate app-level fix (not done, it is app code):* check for matching enabled
   webhooks before serializing in `WebhookService#call`. That would also help
   production, not just tests.

3. **Devise password hashing (about 3000 bcrypt digests per run, about 8% of CPU
   once 1 and 2 were fixed).**
   Every user built by a fabricator hashes its password, and every local account
   builds a user, so every `Fabricate(:status)` (which builds a local account) hashes
   too. A minimum-cost bcrypt digest (`stretches = 1` in test is clamped to bcrypt's
   minimum cost of 4) takes about 1.2 ms and cannot be made cheaper.
   *Fix (model specs only):* `spec/support/test_performance.rb` memoizes
   `Devise::Encryptor.digest` per (model class, pepper, stretches, password). Only the
   salt is shared, and `valid_password?` still verifies correctly. Checked that no
   spec in `spec/models` expects distinct digests for equal passwords. The only
   `encrypted_password` `change` expectations live in `spec/controllers`.
"
}

     does not apply to `sql`). Removing it needs `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber.detach_from :active_record`,

     (`.github/workflows/test-ruby.yml`), so SQL debugging data is kept for now. This is
     the cheapest remaining lever if more speed is needed.
   - *GC (about 8-10% of CPU).* Not tunable at runtime. Only via environment
     variables such as `RUBY_GC_HEAP_INIT_SLOTS` / `RUBY_GC_MALLOC_LIMIT`, set before
     boot. Not measured yet.
   - *Mailer rendering on user creation (about 4% ActionMailer, about 2% Premailer).*
     Devise notifications render HTML and inline CSS. Changing that would change what
     specs see in mail bodies.
   - *Media/image processing (Paperclip, Vips, ffmpeg, about 3%).* Specs assert on
     real thumbnails and metadata. Keep.
   - *App validators that query the DB for each user (`UsernameBlock`,
     `EmailDomainBlock`, `UnreservedUsernameValidator`, `UniqueUsernameValidator`,
     about 9% combined, inclusive, overlapping parts not summed).* App code, so not touched.
   - *`Setting` reads (about 2-4%).* `config.after` clears `Rails.cache` after every
     example. Keeping the cache across examples would return rolled-back settings, so
     this stays.
   - *Fabricators (out of scope until phase 3).* `account` fabricator builds a `user`
     for every local account. `status` fabricator builds an account when none is given
     and creates a bookmark in `after_create`. Inclusive cost in the phase-1 profile:
     the `status` fabricator's `after_create` bookmark block about 18%, the `account`
     fabricator's `user` build about 9%.
     The `account` fabricator attaches a precomputed keypair, so RSA key generation
     (`Account#generate_keys`, about 19 ms per key) is avoided. Keep it that way.

module SignedRequestHelpers
  def get(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "get #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")

    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end

  def post(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    headers['Digest'] = "SHA-256=#{Digest::SHA256.base64digest(args[:params].to_s)}"

    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "post #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date', 'Digest')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")
    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end
end

module DomainHelpers
  def configure_mx(domain:, exchange:, ip_v4_addr: '2.3.4.5', ip_v6_addr: 'fd00::2')
    resolver = instance_double(Resolv::DNS, :timeouts= => nil)

    allow(resolver).to receive(:getresources)
      .with(domain, Resolv::DNS::Resource::IN::MX)
      .and_return([double_mx(exchange)])
    allow(resolver)
      .to receive(:getresources)
      .with(domain, Resolv::DNS::Resource::IN::A)
      .and_return([])
    allow(resolver)
      .to receive(:getresources)
      .with(domain, Resolv::DNS::Resource::IN::AAAA)
      .and_return([])
    allow(resolver)
      .to receive(:getresources)
      .with(exchange, Resolv::DNS::Resource::IN::A)
      .and_return([double_resource_v4(ip_v4_addr)])
    allow(resolver)
      .to receive(:getresources)
      .with(exchange, Resolv::DNS::Resource::IN::AAAA)
      .and_return([double_resource_v6(ip_v6_addr)])
    allow(Resolv::DNS)
      .to receive(:open)
      .and_yield(resolver)
  end

  def configure_dns(domain:, results:)
    resolver = instance_double(Resolv::DNS, :timeouts= => nil)

    allow(resolver).to receive(:getresources)
      .with(domain, Resolv::DNS::Resource::IN::MX)
      .and_return(results)
    allow(resolver)
      .to receive(:getresources)
      .with(domain, Resolv::DNS::Resource::IN::A)
      .and_return(results)
    allow(resolver)
      .to receive(:getresources)
      .with(domain, Resolv::DNS::Resource::IN::AAAA)
      .and_return(results)
    allow(Resolv::DNS)
      .to receive(:open)
      .and_yield(resolver)
  end

  def local_domain_uri
    Addressable::URI.parse("//#{Rails.configuration.x.local_domain}")
  end

  private

  def double_mx(exchange)
    instance_double(Resolv::DNS::Resource::MX, exchange: exchange)

  def double_resource_v4(addr)
    instance_double(Resolv::DNS::Resource::IN::A, address: addr)
  end

  def double_resource_v6(addr)
    instance_double(Resolv::DNS::Resource::IN::AAAA, address: addr)
  end

require 'concurrent/atomic/cyclic_barrier'

module ThreadingHelpers
  def multi_threaded_execution(thread_count)
    barrier = Concurrent::CyclicBarrier.new(thread_count)

    threads = Array.new(thread_count) do |index|
      Thread.new do
        barrier.wait
        yield(index)
      end
    end

    threads.each(&:join)
  end
end

steps.message: The CLI self-time view is flat, so the inclusive view is more useful here. I'll parse the raw dump with `Marshal` and count each frame once per sample, as the phase-1 doc recommends.

arguments.command:
cat > /tmp/sp_incl.rb <<'EOF'
# Inclusive (each frame counted once per sample) and self sample shares from a raw stackprof dump.
dump = Marshal.load(File.binread(ARGV[0]))
top = (ARGV[1] || 60).to_i
frames = dump[:frames]
raw = dump[:raw]
total = 0
incl = Hash.new(0)
selfc = Hash.new(0)
i = 0
while i < raw.size
  len = raw[i]
  stack = raw[i + 1, len]
  count = raw[i + 1 + len]
  i += len + 2
  total += count
  seen = {}
  stack.each do |fid|
    key = fid
    next if seen[key]
    seen[key] = true
    incl[key] += count
  end
  selfc[stack.first] += count
end
label = ->(fid) { f = frames[fid]; "#{f[:name]} (#{File.basename(f[:file].to_s)}:#{f[:line]})" }
File.open(ARGV[2] || '/tmp/incl.txt', 'w') do |out|
  out.puts "total samples: #{total}"
  out.puts "\n== INCLUSIVE"
  incl.sort_by { |_, c| -c }.first(top).each { |fid, c| out.printf("%6.2f%%  %6.2f%% self  %s\n", 100.0 * c / total, 100.0 * selfc[fid] / total, label.(fid)) }
end
puts File.read(ARGV[2] || '/tmp/incl.txt')
EOF
cd /tmp && timeout 900 ruby /tmp/sp_incl.rb /tmp/req_orig_cpu.dump 90 /tmp/req_orig_incl.txt 2>&1 | head -100

arguments.command:
cd /tmp && timeout 900 ruby -e '
dump = Marshal.load(File.binread("/tmp/req_orig_cpu.dump")); frames = dump[:frames]; raw = dump[:raw]
total = 0; incl = Hash.new(0); selfc = Hash.new(0); i = 0
while i < raw.size
  len = raw[i]; stack = raw[i+1, len]; count = raw[i+1+len]; i += len + 2; total += count
  stack.uniq.each { |fid| incl[fid] += count }
  selfc[stack.first] += count
end
File.open("/tmp/req_orig_incl_all.txt","w") do |out|
  out.puts "total #{total}"
  incl.sort_by { |_, c| -c }.each { |fid, c| f = frames[fid]; out.printf("%7.2f%% %7.2f%%self  %s  [%s:%s]\n", 100.0*c/total, 100.0*selfc[fid]/total, f[:name], File.basename(f[:file].to_s), f[:line]) }
end
Marshal.dump({total: total}, File.open("/tmp/req_orig_total.bin","wb"))
' && wc -l /tmp/req_orig_incl_all.txt && grep -iE "webhook|verbose|BCrypt|Devise|Encryptor|LogSubscriber|generate_keys|keypair|OpenSSL|RSA|Premailer|Mail|render|Paperclip|Vips|ffmpeg|Chewy|elastic|Setting|Rails.cache|Redis|Sidekiq|Nokogiri|JSON|Oj|Serializ|GC|garbage|sweep|mark" /tmp/req_orig_incl_all.txt | head -150

# usage: ruby sp_callers.rb dump regex [depth]
# For samples whose stack contains a frame matching regex, tally the caller chain (ancestors, nearest first)
# and the nearest spec file frame. Stacks in stackprof raw dumps are leaf-first.
dump = Marshal.load(File.binread(ARGV[0]))
re = Regexp.new(ARGV[1])
depth = (ARGV[2] || 6).to_i
frames = dump[:frames]; raw = dump[:raw]
lbl = ->(fid) { f = frames[fid]; "#{f[:name]} (#{File.basename(f[:file].to_s)}:#{f[:line]})" }
total = 0; hit = 0
chains = Hash.new(0); specs = Hash.new(0)
i = 0
while i < raw.size
  len = raw[i]; stack = raw[i + 1, len]; count = raw[i + 1 + len]; i += len + 2
  total += count
  idx = stack.index { |fid| frames[fid][:name] =~ re }
  next unless idx
  hit += count
  anc = stack[(idx + 1)...(idx + 1 + depth)].map { |fid| lbl.(fid) }
  chains[anc.join("  <-  ")] += count
  sp = stack[idx..].find { |fid| frames[fid][:file].to_s =~ /_spec\.rb|spec\/support/ }
  specs[sp ? lbl.(sp) : '(no spec frame)'] += count
end
printf("matched %.2f%% of samples\n", 100.0 * hit / total)
puts "\n== top caller chains"
chains.sort_by { |_, c| -c }.first(12).each { |k, c| printf("%6.2f%%  %s\n", 100.0 * c / total, k) }
puts "\n== nearest spec frame"
specs.sort_by { |_, c| -c }.first(15).each { |k, c| printf("%6.2f%%  %s\n", 100.0 * c / total, k) }
EOF

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > spec/support/test_performance.rb <<'EOF'
# frozen_string_literal: true

# Configuration-level guards that keep the test suite fast.
# Background, baseline metrics and the optimization plan live in docs/rspec-performance.md.

RSpec.configure do |config|
  # Spec types that get the webhook and password guards below. Widen this list only
  # after checking the assertions of the other spec types (see docs/rspec-performance.md).
  performance_guard_types = %i(model request).freeze

  # Verbose query logs make ActiveRecord capture and clean a backtrace for every
  # SQL statement the suite runs (~35% of spec/models CPU time). The Rails default
  # is `false`; nothing in the suite asserts on log output, so keep it off per
  # example, even if a spec file flips the global at load time.
  config.before do
    ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs = false
  end

  # Creating a local User or Status enqueues TriggerWebhookWorker, which Sidekiq
  # runs inline in specs. WebhookService serializes the event *before* looking up
  # enabled webhooks, so in most specs (no enabled webhook) ~25% of spec/models CPU
  # and ~23% of spec/requests CPU went into building a payload that is never
  # delivered. When no webhook is enabled the job has no observable effect, so skip
  # it. Specs that create an enabled webhook still run the real pipeline. Specs that
  # stub perform_async themselves are unaffected, since their stubs are defined after
  # this one.
  config.before do |example|
    next unless performance_guard_types.include?(example.metadata[:type])

    allow(TriggerWebhookWorker).to receive(:perform_async).and_wrap_original do |original, *args|
      original.call(*args) if Webhook.enabled.exists?
    end
  end

  # Devise bcrypt-hashes the password of every user built by a fabricator (~1.2ms
  # each, even at bcrypt's minimum cost of 4), and local accounts build a user too,
  # so a spec run hashed thousands of times. Specs only use a few passwords, and
  # `valid_password?` still verifies a memoized digest, so reuse one digest per
  # (model, pepper, stretches, password). Only the random salt is shared.
  password_digests = {}
  config.before do |example|
    next unless performance_guard_types.include?(example.metadata[:type])

module Rails
  class Application
    class RoutesReloader
      include ActiveSupport::Callbacks

      attr_reader :route_sets, :paths, :external_routes, :loaded
      attr_accessor :eager_load
      attr_writer :run_after_load_paths, :loaded # :nodoc:
      delegate :execute_if_updated, :updated?, to: :updater

      def initialize
        @paths      = []
        @route_sets = []
        @external_routes = []
        @eager_load = false
        @loaded = false

        clear!
        load_paths
        finalize!
        route_sets.each(&:eager_load!) if eager_load
      ensure
        revert
      end

      def execute
        @loaded = true
        updater.execute
      end

        unless @loaded
          execute
          ActiveSupport.run_load_hooks(:after_routes_loaded, Rails.application)
          true
        end
      end

        end
      end

        route_sets.each do |routes|
          routes.disable_clear_and_finalize = true
          routes.clear!

        run_after_load_paths.call

arguments.command:
cd /app && cat > spec/support/before_all_examples.rb <<'EOF'
# frozen_string_literal: true

# Creates records once for a whole example group instead of once per example.
#
#   describe 'Something' do
#     before_all_examples do
#       Fabricate(:account, username: 'alice')
#     end
#
#     let(:alice) { Account.find_by(username: 'alice') }
#   end
#
# The block runs in `before(:context)`. Its writes stay in a transaction that is
# rolled back in `after(:context)`. Each example still runs in its own savepoint
# (rspec-rails transactional fixtures), so an example's changes are rolled back before
# the next example runs, as they are with a per-example `before` block.
#
# Limits:
# * Use it only for records that every example in the group can share. Examples should
#   read them from the database (for example with `let`), not keep Ruby objects that
#   they change in memory.
# * State outside the database is not covered. Redis and Rails.cache are not rolled
#   back, and rails_helper clears Redis after every example, so the shared block's
#   Redis state would be gone after the first example.
# * RSpec mocks are not usable in `before(:context)`. The guards in
#   spec/support/test_performance.rb therefore do not apply to the shared block.
# * Do not use it in groups with examples that set `use_transactional_tests: false`.
module SharedFixtures
  def before_all_examples(&block)
    before(:context) do
      # Pin the primary connection the same way rspec-rails pins it for each example.
      # The pin opens a transaction that example transactions nest in as savepoints,
      # and it stops example teardown from returning the connection to the pool.
      ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.pin_connection!(true)
      instance_exec(&block)
    end

    after(:context) do
      ActiveRecord::Base.connection_pool.unpin_connection!
    end
  end
end

RSpec.configure do |config|
  config.extend SharedFixtures
end

CI settles the question. The main `bin/flatware rspec` job, which runs `spec/models` and `spec/requests`, never archives `log/`. Only the e2e and search jobs do, and those run `spec/system` and `spec/search`, which are different spec types. So the SQL lines from model and request examples are never kept in CI artifacts.

Rails 8.1 formats SQL before checking the log level, so lowering the level wouldn't remove the cost. Detaching the ActiveRecord log subscriber does, and it can be scoped to the model and request types. Before doing that, I'll check that no spec or app code depends on that subscriber's output or runtime counters.

  *Fixed* by widening the guard to `type: :request`.

  `before` block created 7 records (users, statuses, poll, invite, token, follow) for each
  of the 258 examples. This was the largest single file cost (34 s). *Fixed* with the
  `before_all_examples` helper: the records are built once per group, and the examples
  still run in their own transactions. File time now about 4 s.

  5 s per run).** `after { Rails.application.reload_routes! }` ran after each of 30 examples
  and each reload loads all routes. Every example already stubs the routes in `before`, so
  restoring once per group is equivalent. *Fixed* with `after(:context)`. File time 6.2 s
  -> 0.6 s.

  request specs. No request spec checks distinct digests (the only `encrypted_password`
  override sets an empty string explicitly).

  every statement even though nothing reads it in `spec/models` and `spec/requests`. Those
  spec types never produce CI log artifacts (only the e2e and search jobs archive `log/`),
  so the subscriber is detached while their examples run. *Fixed* in
  `spec/support/test_performance.rb`. Profile after the change: `LogSubscriber#sql` 6.6% ->
  0.02% of samples.

  - *Fabricators (about 41% inclusive, the largest remaining item).* `status`, `account`,
    `user` and the bookmark `after_create` callback. Phase 3 (factories).
  - *GC (about 9-11% of CPU).* Only tunable through `RUBY_GC_*` environment variables set
    before boot (CI config). `GC.config` exposes only `rgengc_allow_full_mark`. Not measured.

    and Devise mails. Some specs assert on mail bodies, so this stays.
  - *Fan-out (about 5.5%).* `DistributionWorker` and `FanOutOnWriteService` with
    `RedisLock`. Feeds are asserted, so this stays.
  - *Shared setup in `activitypub/replies_spec.rb` (7 s) and the notifications specs (6 s
    and 4 s).* Their fixtures depend on `let`s that vary per context, or they create
    Redis-backed feeds. Restructuring them is possible but needs care (see the Gotchas).
  - *`support/examples/api.rb` (about 9 s).* The cost is each caller's setup plus its request.
  - *Rack, Warden, I18n and `Localized#set_locale` show large inclusive shares.* They wrap
    the whole request, so they are not a cost on their own.
  - *`Setting` reads (about 2%).* `Rails.cache` is cleared after each example (see phase 1).
